site.name: Fennick Lane Community Garden
site.tagline: Growing food, flowers and friendships on a quarter acre of Harrowby
site.intro: We are a group of neighbours who look after a shared garden at the end of Fennick Lane. Some of us have our own plots, some help on the shared beds, and some just come for the tea. Everyone is welcome.
site.meet: Work days are on Saturday mornings, roughly every fortnight from March to October. Just turn up at the lane gate.
site.demo_note: Fennick Lane Community Garden is fictional. This site is a demonstration built for newsroom.sgit.ai to show a small website that its owners can edit by talking to Claude.
site.studio_link_text: Built by Kitewing Websites, a made-up studio

grow.name: Vegetables
grow.text: Tomatoes, courgettes, beans, potatoes, salad and squash on the shared beds and members' plots.

grow.name: Herbs
grow.text: A herb spiral by the shed with mint, chives, thyme, sage and parsley. Take a sprig when you need one.

grow.name: Fruit
grow.text: Four old apple trees in the orchard corner, a row of raspberries and a rhubarb patch that never gives up.

grow.name: Flowers
grow.text: Sunflowers, calendula and sweet peas for cutting, and wildflowers along the lane for the bees.

grow.name: Wildlife
grow.text: A small pond, a bug hotel, a hedge and a wild corner where nettles feed the butterflies.

grow.name: Community
grow.text: Tea in the shed, shared tools, a seed tin, and a table by the gate for spare produce.

plots.summary: The garden has 18 half-size plots, 4 shared beds and a raised bed for members who prefer not to kneel.
plots.waiting: Plots are offered in order from the waiting list each autumn, when members decide whether to carry on. In the meantime you are very welcome on the shared beds, which is how most plot holders started.
steps: Come to any work day and say hello at the shed.
Ask a committee member to add your name to the waiting list book.
Help on the shared beds while you wait, if you like.
When a plot comes free, we will find you at the next work day or leave a note on the gate board.
plots.note: The waiting list is kept in a paper book in the shed, not online, so nobody's details are published here.

events.title: Spring clear-up and soup
events.blurb: We clear winter debris, turn the compost bays and mend the path edges. Leek and potato soup at one o'clock.

events.title: Seed swap at the shed
events.blurb: Bring spare seed, saved or shop-bought, and leave with something new to try. Envelopes and pencils provided.

events.title: Potato planting morning
events.blurb: First earlies go in on the shared beds. A good one for first-timers: we show you trenching and spacing.

events.title: Children's sunflower race begins
events.blurb: Every child plants a sunflower seed in a named pot. We measure them in July and everybody gets a rosette.

events.title: Plant sale for the garden fund
events.blurb: Tomato, courgette and herb plants raised by members, all sold for a small donation to the garden fund.

events.title: Pond dipping and wildlife count
events.blurb: Nets, trays and identification cards. We record what we find in the garden notebook.

events.title: Watering rota briefing
events.blurb: Before the dry weeks arrive we agree who waters what, and how to use the water butts fairly.

events.title: Midsummer picnic
events.blurb: Bring a dish to share. Lanterns, a little music and a walk round the plots to see how everyone is getting on.

events.title: Sunflower measuring day
events.blurb: The tape measure comes out. Tallest, cheeriest and most lopsided sunflowers each get a home-made rosette.

events.title: Open garden afternoon
events.blurb: Neighbours welcome. Members show their plots, the shed serves tea and there is a table of spare courgettes.

events.title: Pickling and preserving workshop
events.blurb: Quick pickles, a simple chutney and how to store a glut safely. Jars to take home.

events.title: Harvest supper
events.blurb: A shared supper cooked from the garden. Long tables, a harvest display and thanks to every volunteer.

events.title: Bulb planting and hedge day
events.blurb: Daffodils along the lane and fifty new hedge whips for the birds. Spades and tea provided.

events.title: Apple pressing
events.blurb: Bring windfalls from home. We wash, scrat and press them, and everyone leaves with a bottle of juice.

events.title: Season close and AGM
events.blurb: A short annual meeting, the waiting list update and plans for next year. Cake, of course.

rota.intro: Volunteers sign up for a fortnight at a time. Names here are invented for the demonstration. The real rota is the chalkboard on the shed door.

news.title: New water butts on the shed roof
news.text: Thanks to the summer plant sale we have fitted two more water butts. That nearly doubles what we can collect from the shed roof.

news.title: A record sunflower
news.text: This year's tallest sunflower, grown on the children's bed, finished taller than the shed door. It now lives on as bird food.

news.title: Open afternoon thank you
news.text: Neighbours came to look round, several new names went in the waiting list book and the courgette table emptied by four o'clock.

news.title: Hedgehog spotted
news.text: A hedgehog has been seen near the compost bays at dusk. Please check the bays before turning them and keep the gap under the gate clear.

guides.title: Your first plot: where to start
guides.lead: A new plot can look like a lot. Start small and you will enjoy it more.
steps: Walk the plot and note where the sun falls in the morning and the afternoon.
Clear one bed properly rather than four beds badly.
Cover the rest with cardboard to stop weeds while you work up to it.
Choose three easy crops for your first season: salad leaves, courgettes and beans.
Ask a neighbour on the next plot. Everyone here was new once.
guides.tip: Bring a flask to the garden. Plots are friendlier when you sit down on them now and then.

guides.title: Making compost in the shared bays
guides.lead: Our three compost bays turn kitchen and garden waste into the soil we all share.
steps: Mix greens (peelings, grass, soft prunings) with browns (cardboard, straw, dry leaves).
Aim for roughly equal amounts of each by volume.
Chop big stems so they rot down faster.
Leave out cooked food, meat, dairy and diseased plants.
We turn the bays together on work days. You are welcome to join in.
guides.tip: If the heap smells, it needs more browns. If nothing is happening, it needs more greens and a little water.

guides.title: Growing tomatoes outdoors
guides.lead: Tomatoes like warmth, shelter and steady watering. Harrowby summers can do the job.
steps: Plant out after the last frost, usually late May here.
Choose a sunny spot sheltered from the wind off the lane.
Push in a stout cane at planting time so you do not damage roots later.
Pinch out side shoots on cordon types as they appear.
Water at the base, little and often, rather than soaking now and then.
guides.tip: Uneven watering causes split fruit. A water butt nearby makes regular watering much easier.

guides.title: Courgettes without the glut panic
guides.lead: Two plants feed a family. Six plants feed the street.
steps: Sow indoors in late April, one seed on its edge per pot.
Plant out in June into a rich, well-watered spot.
Pick when fruit are the length of your hand. They grow fast.
Check every two days in summer, or they will turn into marrows.
Share spares on the table by the gate.
guides.tip: Leave space around each plant: they spread more than the seed packet suggests.

guides.title: Runner beans up a wigwam
guides.lead: A wigwam of canes takes little space and gives beans from July to the first frosts.
steps: Push six to eight long canes into a circle and tie them at the top.
Sow two seeds at the foot of each cane in late May.
Keep the one that comes up stronger.
Water well when the flowers appear, so they set pods.
Pick often. The more you pick, the more they make.
guides.tip: Children love a bean wigwam with a gap left for a door. It becomes a den by August.

guides.title: Salad leaves all summer
guides.lead: Small sowings every few weeks give you leaves to cut from spring to autumn.
steps: Sow a short row every three weeks from April to August.
Choose cut-and-come-again mixes for easy picking.
Give them a little shade in the hottest weeks.
Cut leaves with scissors a thumb's width above the soil.
Water in the evening during dry spells.
guides.tip: Slugs love young leaves. See the guide on slugs for kind ways to keep them off.

guides.title: Potatoes for beginners
guides.lead: Potatoes are forgiving, and digging them up feels like treasure hunting.
steps: Set seed potatoes in egg boxes in a light, cool room to sprout in February.
Plant first earlies in early April, about a trowel deep.
Draw soil up around the stems as they grow. This is called earthing up.
First earlies are usually ready when the flowers open.
Dig carefully from the side of the row with a fork.
guides.tip: Keep potatoes covered by soil: green potatoes should not be eaten.

guides.title: Watering wisely in dry weeks
guides.lead: Our water comes from butts and one shared tap, so we use it carefully.
steps: Water in the early morning or evening, not at midday.
Water the roots, not the leaves.
One good soak twice a week beats a sprinkle every day.
Mulch around plants with grass clippings or compost to hold moisture.
Follow the rota on the shed door during holidays.
guides.tip: Seedlings and new plantings come first when water is short. Established shrubs can usually wait.

guides.title: Living with slugs, kindly
guides.lead: We garden without slug pellets to protect the frogs and birds that help us.
steps: Go out with a torch on damp evenings and move slugs to the wild corner.
Raise seedlings in pots until they are sturdy before planting out.
Use collars cut from plastic bottles around young plants.
Encourage frogs: our pond is their headquarters.
Accept a few holes. The garden is shared with wildlife too.
guides.tip: Beer traps work, but sink them a little proud of the soil so beetles can climb out.

guides.title: Flowers for bees and hoverflies
guides.lead: Flowers among the veg bring the insects that pollinate our crops.
steps: Sow calendula and cornflowers at the ends of your beds.
Let a few herbs flower: chives, thyme and marjoram.
Leave dandelions in the wild corner for early bees.
Plant for a long season, from crocus in spring to ivy in autumn.
Skip sprays. Insects eat the pests for us.
guides.tip: Sunflowers are the garden's favourite: tall, cheerful and full of seed for the birds in autumn.

guides.title: Saving your own seeds
guides.lead: Saved seed costs nothing and adapts a little more to our garden every year.
steps: Start with easy ones: peas, beans, tomatoes and sunflowers.
Choose your best plants to save from, not the leftovers.
Let pods dry on the plant until they rattle.
Dry seeds on a plate indoors for a week.
Store in labelled paper envelopes in a cool, dry tin.
guides.tip: Bring spares to the March seed swap and write the variety and year on every envelope.

guides.title: Putting a plot to bed for winter
guides.lead: A little care in autumn makes spring much easier.
steps: Clear spent crops and add healthy ones to the compost.
Spread a layer of compost or leaves over empty beds.
Sow a green manure such as field beans to cover bare soil.
Clean and oil tools before they go in the shed.
Leave some seed heads standing for birds and insects.
guides.tip: Covered soil is happy soil. Bare soil washes away in winter rain.

guides.title: Using the shared tools
guides.lead: The shed holds tools for everyone. A few habits keep them working.
steps: Sign tools out on the board by the door.
Scrape soil off before putting them back.
Report anything broken on the shed whiteboard.
Return wheelbarrows upside down so they do not fill with rain.
Lock the shed if you are the last to leave.
guides.tip: The combination is shared in person at your first work day, never online.

guides.title: Gardening with children
guides.lead: Children are welcome at Fennick Lane when they come with a grown-up.
steps: Give them their own small patch, even one square of a bed.
Choose fast crops: radishes, cress, sunflowers and peas.
Let them water, dig and pick. Mess is part of it.
Show them the pond and the bug hotel.
Join the sunflower race in April.
guides.tip: Small watering cans are hung on the low hooks inside the shed door.

contact.where: The garden is at the end of Fennick Lane, Harrowby, behind the church hall. (Fictional address.)
contact.how: The easiest way to reach us is to come to a work day. There is also a notice board on the lane gate.
